summary: A 3D spaceship game where students fly to the Moon and Mars and visit 8 NASA hardware sites. Each stop has a NASA image and a voice-guided story. It answers the storytelling challenge for school-age space fans.This is important beacuse it is a easier and more applicable way for a children to understand the topics because it is a game.
details:
Abandoned but not Forgotten is a browser-based 3D spaceship game that tells the stories of NASA machines left on the Moon and Mars. It is made for school-age space enthusiasts.

What it does and how it works
The player enters a spaceship cockpit and reads written instructions. A 10-second countdown with a voice assistant follows, and then the ship launches. The player flies freely in any direction using the keyboard. They steer first to the Moon and then to Mars, where eight glowing stations mark real NASA sites:

  • Moon: Apollo 11 (Tranquility Base), Surveyor 3, and Apollo 17.
  • Mars: Viking 1, Mars Pathfinder with Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, and the Ingenuity helicopter.

When the ship reaches a station, the game shows an image from NASA’s Image and Video Library and a short written story. A voice assistant reads the story aloud. Each story covers what the machine did, what it discovered, and how its mission ended. After all eight stations, the game shows a “Game Ended” screen.

Benefits and intended impact
The game turns NASA’s history of exploration into something students can explore for themselves. These machines finished their missions, but their discoveries still matter. Examples are Opportunity’s years of work on Mars, Ingenuity’s first powered flight on another planet, and the Apollo 11 laser reflector that scientists still use today. We want students to see that “abandoned” hardware is part of a continuing story of science. The game is free, needs no install, and runs in a browser, so teachers and students can use it anywhere.

Tools and technology

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single static web page.
  • Three.js for the 3D scene, flight controls, planets and stations.
  • Web Speech API for the voice assistant.
  • Web Audio API for synthesized sound effects (engine hum, countdown beeps, arrival chimes). There is no music.
  • NASA Image and Video Library API (images-api.nasa.gov) for images.
  • GitHub for the code and Render for hosting.
  • No special hardware is needed, only a computer with a modern browser and sound.

Creativity
Instead of a slideshow or a timeline, the player drives to each story. The countdown, flight and arrival give a feeling of a real mission. Voice narration and written text work together so the content is accessible to different learners. The sound design uses only effects, so the narration stays clear.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: mission facts come from NASA mission records, and the images are NASA’s own and credited by title and ID.
  • Age-appropriate learning: short stories in plain language, with clear instructions.
  • Accessibility: every story is available in both text and voice, and the voice can be turned off.
  • Licensing: we used no NASA logos or branding. We credit NASA and state that the project is not endorsed by NASA.
  • Simplicity: planet sizes and distances are shortened so the trip is quick. The game says this on the start screen.
  • AI use: AI (Claude by Anthropic) helped write the code, story text and demo slides. No AI-generated images or video are used
